analysis:
The supplied units are head-side excerpts of docs/reference/protocol-messages.md (lines 579-1250). The only changed range in the patch is head lines 202-219, which adds a documentation section on WebSocket close codes and the reconnect wait. Those lines are not in the supplied text units, so I could not verify that the patch matches the reconnect source. This is a docs-only change: no code, key handling, attestation, authorization, or routing behavior changes.

The documented reconnect behavior is as follows. The provider reads the close-frame code from the coordinator side. Code 1012 gets a delay drawn from serviceRestartDelayRange with no backoff growth. Any other code, or no close frame, uses the growing ExponentialBackoff. A session open for stableSessionDuration or more resets the backoff. Every reconnect sends a fresh register. This is consistent with TB-002 and the existing endpoint-resumption guidance: it grants no trust, does not extend the Apple proof lifetime, and re-registers on every reconnect.

The availability trade-off is worth recording against TB-002. The coordinator is trusted, so the code is trusted. A network-level adversary who forges a close frame cannot do so on a TLS-protected channel. The 1012 path keeps the backoff from growing, so a repeated 1012 could cause tight, jittered reconnect loops. serviceRestartDelayRange is bounded by the source, but I did not see its values. Whether the range prevents a thundering herd is a runtime matter for the next pass to check in CoordinatorReconnectPolicy.swift.

The rest of the supplied text (slots telemetry, performance measurements, service_reservation_released, inference_error sanitization, models_replace, prefix cache v2 receipts) appears to be pre-existing context. I found nothing indicating regressions there. T-041 posture is unchanged: the docs still describe nonce-bound receipts, scope binding, and no per-anchor eviction frames. No finding qualifies. I recommend only a light check of the reconnect policy source against the docs; this is not a security-blocking uncertainty.
